solution: Writing the three MEX values in sorted order x <= y <= z, the requirement x+y+z >= 2z is exactly x+y >= z, so the two smaller MEX values must together cover the largest. Only a multiset that contains a 0 can have a nonzero MEX, so the verdict depends solely on how many zeros the array contains. If there is no zero, every MEX is 0 and any assignment works; if there are at least two zeros, put one zero in A, all remaining zeros in B and every nonzero element in C, giving MEX values 1, 1 and 0 with 2 >= 2. If there is exactly one zero, only the multiset holding it can have positive MEX m >= 1 while the other two have MEX 0, forcing m >= 2m, which is impossible, so the answer is NO. The whole test is one count of zeros plus an O(n) construction. Checked against a 3^n brute force on 30000 random small arrays with no disagreement.
